column17: The paper designs, instantiates and evaluates an artefact: an 'end-to-end generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) framework for automating the generation, adaptation, and evaluation of discrete-event simulation (DES) models in manufacturing' (Abstract, p. 642). Section 4 specifies the workflow (blueprint model, agent roles, HITL checkpoints), Section 5 demonstrates and measures it over 21 experiment runs on two industrial cases, and Section 5.6 validates generated models against reference models. No primary empirical data collection about people or organisations; not a conceptual/vision paper.
column19: Working system exists (Python workflow with OpenAI API calls, SimPy DES models, PM4Py, Mermaid visualisation; full implementation with blueprints, prompts, scripts and Case B input data published on GitHub) and is quantitatively evaluated: 21 experiment runs with per-stage code-correctness and accuracy tallies (Tables 5 and 7, Fig. 18) plus input-output validation of generated models against manually built FACTS Analyzer reference models with predefined acceptance thresholds (Tables 8 and 9, Sargent [46]). Clear case for 'implemented-validated'; the evaluation is nonetheless author-performed on two self-selected cases.
column20: Automotive manufacturing / discrete manufacturing. Two real production lines at 'a large Swedish automotive manufacturer' (Sections 4.2 and 5); author affiliation and competing-interest statement identify the case company as Scania CV AB.
column21: Two production lines: Case A, an automated machining line with four sequential operations and identical intermediate buffers (30-day simulation horizon, 25 replications); Case B, an automated assembly line with seven operations, two presses in parallel, defect rate 8.9% at the Quality station (7-day horizon, 10 replications). Case B is a simplified representation of the system studied in Schmitt et al. [3]; its event log is a mock-up to allow public data sharing. Objectives: productivity (TH), energy efficiency (SEC) and inventory (WIP).
column22: Two numbered RQs (p. 643): RQ1: 'How can LLMs be applied to generate, adapt, and evaluate simulations of manufacturing systems?' RQ2: 'What are the main challenges and benefits associated with implementing LLM-driven simulations?' Stated aim: 'to develop a comprehensive LLM-driven workflow that can automatically generate, modify, and evaluate simulation models, thereby expanding the exploration and analysis of industrial process improvements and providing effective decision support'.
column24: SEVERE BOUNDARY CASE - R1 SHOULD CONSIDER EXCLUSION. The paper addresses DES model generation and scenario evaluation for existing brownfield production lines; improvements are buffer capacities, machine availability, cycle time, MTTR and (in one case) adding a third parallel press. Mapped to 'factory-planning' as the only subdomain in the review's scope that covers production-system/material-flow analysis and capacity dimensioning at factory level, and because the journal scope and the paper's framing sit in manufacturing system design and analysis. However: no VDI 5200 or comparable factory-planning framework is cited; the paper positions itself in the automatic simulation model generation (ASMG) literature [26] and in simulation-based production development [3]; and the decisions supported are predominantly parameter-level improvements of an operating line, which is below the strategic/upper-tactical boundary. Authors themselves note that strict fidelity is required for 'brownfield' cases and that the more strategic 'greenfield' use (higher degrees of freedom, conceptual models) is only an outlook (Section 6.3, p. 657). No supply-chain, site, network or technology-selection content.
column26: Not used. 'simulation-modeling' is the primary and unambiguous mapping (automated generation, adaptation and evaluation of DES models for planning). 'capacity-dimensioning' covers the adaptation content (buffer capacities, machine availability, cycle times, adding a parallel press to lift line capacity); 'material-flow-design' covers the part-flow logic extracted by process mining and modelled/adapted by the agents (serial/parallel routing, splitter-merger logic, defect sinks). If R1 prefers a minimal coding, 'simulation-modeling' alone is defensible, since capacity and flow changes are outputs of the simulation study rather than a separately formulated planning task.
column29: No planning horizon is stated anywhere. The only explicit time spans are simulation run lengths (30-day horizon with 1-day warm-up for Case A; 7-day horizon with 1-day warm-up for Case B) and execution times (~20 min / ~10 min per experiment), which are model parameters, not planning horizons. Substance leans tactical/operational: the workflow analyses two operating lines and proposes parameter-level improvements to bottleneck machines and buffers, with 'Implement and evaluate changes in production' as the downstream step (Fig. 1). A structural reading is possible for the Case B adaptation that adds a third parallel press (capacity expansion, investment-relevant) and for the authors' 'greenfield' outlook. Coded 'ambiguous'; R1 decision needed, including whether the study meets the review's strategic-scope inclusion criterion at all.
column31: The authors never frame the decision as system-configuring, and the majority of supported decisions concern how existing resources perform rather than what exists: buffer capacity, availability, cycle time, MTTR and defect-rate parameters of an existing line (Tables 5 and 7). Two elements point the other way and should be weighed by R1: (i) adaptations are explicitly graded into three complexity levels, including 'intermediate complexity for structural adaptations (e.g., adding or removing operations)' and 'high complexity for modifying the underlying operational logic' (Section 4.3.3, p. 648); and (ii) in every Case B experiment a manually added suggestion to 'add a third parallel press with its own pre-buffer instance' was implemented, which does determine what equipment exists in the line (Fig. 14, V4, +49.9% TH). Coded FALSE because the framing is absent and the structural case is one configurable suggestion among mostly parametric ones.
column33: No strategic-planning framework (VDI 5200, SC Planning Matrix, Lanza et al., Wiendahl-Nyhuis, Melo et al.) is cited. The frameworks actually used are: (1) the four-step simulation-based production development process of Schmitt et al. [3] - case definition, current-state analysis, future-state prediction, decision support - which structures the whole workflow (Section 2.2 and Fig. 1); (2) Sargent's verification and validation framework for simulation models [46]; (3) Cimino et al.'s ASMG taxonomy [26] for positioning; and (4) Anthropic's workflow-versus-agent distinction [13] for the agentic design. Theory of constraints [44] underpins the bottleneck definition. R1 may prefer 'none', since none of these is a strategic-planning theory in the sense of section 3.3.
column34: An end-to-end LLM-driven workflow (a 'workflow' in Anthropic's sense [13]: a predefined code path with individual LLM calls, explicitly not an autonomous agent system) that turns heterogeneous production data into executable DES models, adapted scenarios and natural-language decision support. Four stages (Figs. 1-4): (i) input data analysis - static Python, no LLM: machine performance metrics (cycle time, availability, MTTR, idle/processing power) computed from MES event logs, part-flow logic mined with PM4Py, plus manual text inputs for buffer capacities, shift calendar, defects and critical process definitions (CPDs); (ii) model generation - a builder-agent adapts a predefined, generalised Python/SimPy blueprint model to the case using natural-language instructions and a structured parameter set (one-shot), an inspector-agent verifies and repairs the generated code (evaluator-optimizer loop), a visualizer-agent converts the model into Mermaid/JavaScript for a process-flow chart, and the human operator must review and may repair the model before execution; the model is then run for a defined number of replications with warm-up; (iii) model adaptation - a deterministic utilization-based bottleneck analysis feeds a bottleneck-agent that emits JSON improvement instructions (three by default, configurable, plus an optional human suggestion), a CPD-agent checks the suggestions against explicit process constraints and warns the operator, and separate adaptor-agent instances implement each suggestion zero-shot into a new model, again inspected and repaired; (iv) model evaluation - KPIs (throughput, WIP, specific energy consumption) are averaged across replications, charted, and an evaluator-agent produces a textual comparison of current-state and adapted models with an explicit recommendation and trade-off discussion for the human decision-maker, who verifies it. Inputs: event logs, consumption data, defect rates, CPDs, production calendar, blueprint. Outputs: executable SimPy models, process-flow charts, CPD warnings, N adapted scenario models with KPIs, and a natural-language recommendation. 6+N API calls per run (5+N for Case A).
column35: ["GPT-5.1 (OpenAI, via API)", "GPT-5-mini (OpenAI, via API)", "GPT-4o (OpenAI, via API)"]
column36: Task-specific assignment based on SWE-bench performance and cost (Section 4.1.1, Table 2): GPT-5.1, the best-performing evaluated model, for the most demanding tasks - builder- and inspector-agents (initial model generation and code repair); GPT-5-mini, the cheaper lightweight model, for simpler tasks - visualizer-agent (Python to JavaScript flow chart), adaptor- and inspector-agents (parametric and structural changes), evaluator- and CPD-agents (natural-language summaries); GPT-4o for the bottleneck-agent because of its support for structured output (JSON instructions). Listings 2 and 3 confirm model='gpt-5.1' for the builder and model='gpt-5-mini' for the adaptor. 'All LLMs were executed using their default API parameters, including standard context limits and internal sampling settings for, e.g., temperature and top_p' (Fig. 2 caption, p. 647). The setup is stated to be model-agnostic; OpenAI was chosen because of the case company's enterprise access. No cross-model comparison was run; hallucinations were analysed at task level, not per model.
column40: All three models are proprietary OpenAI models accessed through the API (Section 4.1.1; Listings 2-3). No open-weight model is used anywhere, including for embeddings - the workflow contains no retrieval/embedding component. Anthropic and Google models are named only as interchangeable alternatives.
column42: No weight updates. Techniques are zero-, one- and few-shot prompting, prompt engineering/refinement and evaluator-optimizer loops (Section 4.1.2): the builder-agent is one-shot, guided by the blueprint model as the single example of the desired structure; the adaptor-agent operates zero-shot from the current model plus a natural-language instruction. Prompts were iteratively refined across runs to suppress verbose code scaffolding, unclear routing logic and generic simulation patterns (Table 10); two full prompts are published (Listings 2-3) and the complete prompt set is on GitHub. Domain-specialised or SimPy-fine-tuned models are discussed only as expected future improvements (Section 6.1, p. 656) and therefore not coded as applied.
column45: LLM + discrete-event simulation coupling within a deterministic orchestration workflow: LLM calls generate and modify executable SimPy code that is then run by the simulation engine, with the numeric simulation output fed back to an LLM for interpretation, and with an evaluator-optimizer (generator/inspector) loop for code repair. The controlled vocabulary has no 'LLM+simulation' or 'evaluator-optimizer/workflow-graph' term; 'LLM+solver' would misdescribe it (no solver, no optimisation model) and 'LLM+digital-twin' would over-claim (the authors explicitly treat DTs as related but distinct work [21-24,32]). 'multi-agent' is coded because six to seven functionally distinct agent roles (builder, inspector, visualizer, bottleneck, CPD, adaptor, evaluator) interact over shared artefacts, while noting the authors' own caveat that these are 'individual LLM calls integrated into the workflow', not autonomous agents (Section 2.1, p. 644).
column50: NR. No mathematical solver. Software used: SimPy (Python DES library) for the generated models, FACTS Analyzer (commercial C++-based simulation software) for the manually built reference models, PM4Py for process mining.
column51: No optimisation model is formulated: no decision variables, objective function, constraint set or solver appears. Improvement candidates are produced by an LLM from a ranked list of bottlenecks, where the ranking comes from a deterministic utilization analysis embedded in the blueprint; the authors state that 'the utilization-based bottleneck detection is included solely to provide structured input for the LLM; the study does not aim to compare or advance BT detection methods' (Section 4.3.3, p. 648). Evaluation of the resulting scenarios is a manual/LLM-mediated trade-off between three KPIs (TH, WIP, SEC), not a multi-objective optimisation. Design of experiments and optimisation modules are named only as future extensions ('Integrating design of experiments (DOE) or optimization modules could extend the workflow's ability to explore broader search spaces', Section 6.4, p. 657), and simulation-based optimisation appears only in the authors' prior work [3]. AMBIGUITY: because DES itself belongs to the OR tradition and the workflow embeds theory-of-constraints bottleneck analysis [44], R1 could instead code optimization_tradition_present = TRUE with formalization_level = 'low-formalization'; coded FALSE/none here because no optimisation component exists in the system.

column123: The workflow automatically generated executable and valid DES models of two real production lines, proposed and implemented modifications, flagged CPD violations and produced coherent natural-language evaluations. Model generation was the weak link: across 21 runs one crashed and five required manual correction, with Case B (parallel stations) showing more structural errors than Case A (~64% vs ~80% first-pass correctness), mainly in splitting and merging part flows; one Case A run invented a parallel station that existed only in the blueprint example, illustrating overgeneralisation from insufficiently specific instructions. Downstream stages were far more reliable: bottlenecks were consistently identified, CPD violations were flagged in every experiment (including the correct non-flagging of compliant suggestions), adaptations succeeded in all but two instances (one timeout, one logically inconsistent suggestion, which the adaptor-agent nonetheless implemented in the intended direction), and the evaluator-agent correctly interpreted results and weighed trade-offs in every run (evaluation accuracy 100% in both cases). Adapted scenarios yielded modest improvements in Case A (best: +4.5% TH, -1.8% SEC at +7.4% WIP) and substantial ones in Case B, where the manually injected third-parallel-press suggestion gave +49.9% TH and ~16% lower energy per part at +23.3% WIP, with a WIP-neutral alternative at +9.8% TH. Validity: deviations from manually built FACTS Analyzer models averaged -3.9% (TH), 2.0% (SEC) and 3.8% (WIP) for Case A and below 1% on all three metrics for Case B, inside the predefined 5-10% threshold. Cost and speed: ~$0.13-0.16 and ~10-20 min per experiment producing four to five executable models. The authors conclude that LLMs can lower the expertise barrier for DES while output consistency, reproducibility and generalisability to complex systems remain open, and that reliability depends on the blueprint, prompt refinement, evaluator-optimizer loops and human checkpoints rather than on the LLM alone. STUDY DESIGN NOTE: coded 'developer-reported' because the authors designed the workflow, ran all experiments and classified all correctness outcomes themselves with no blinding or independent rater; R1 may prefer 'single-case' (two industrial cases) or 'quasi-experimental' (systematic repeated runs with a reference comparator and varied complexity levels).
column126: HITL is an explicit design element with three named checkpoints (Section 4.1.3, p. 646; Fig. 1): (1) 'Mandatory inspection of the initial simulation model' - the operator inspects the generated model and repairs it if necessary before execution, because generation is the most error-prone step and determines all downstream cost; a manual fix was actually needed in 6 of 21 runs; (2) 'Optional improvement suggestion' - the operator may add a suggestion to those of the bottleneck-agent, because the LLM lacks access to layout, space and cost constraints (used in every Case B experiment: 'add a third parallel press', which became the best-performing scenario); (3) 'Mandatory check of results' - the operator verifies the evaluator-agent's interpretation to catch hallucinations. The CPD-agent additionally 'passes information to the human operator via text' when a suggestion violates a critical process definition, and the operator retains the final trade-off decision. Authors frame these as 'governance mechanisms to ensure reliability rather than as functional dependencies of the method' (p. 646) and align them with Anthropic's agentic best practice [13]. Coded 'approval-gate' because two of the three checkpoints are mandatory human validations gating execution and use of the output; note that checkpoint (2) is a human-injected scenario/what-if element and the CPD warnings are an escalation-style notification, so R1 could add a second type or code 'other' for the combined governance pattern.
column130: Domain knowledge is formalised as executable code and structured constraints, not as an ontology, knowledge graph or encoded standard. (1) The generic blueprint model - 'perhaps this study's most crucial element' (Section 5.1) - is a Python/SimPy template encoding the domain semantics of a production line: Machine and DelayBuffer classes, serial and parallel topologies with splitter and merger routing, part generation and movement, production schedule/shift logic, exponential failure and MTTR distributions, defect rates and sinks, and KPI (TH/WIP/SEC) computation; it supplies the one-shot example that the builder-agent adapts (excerpt in Listing 1; full code on GitHub). The authors explicitly present this as feeding domain-specific knowledge to a generically trained LLM to reduce hallucination. (2) Critical process definitions (CPDs) formalise explicit process constraints (e.g., press process time >= 60 s; all buffer capacities kept at original level) in structured text, checked by a dedicated CPD-agent against each proposed adaptation. (3) Structured parameter inputs: station tables, buffer lists with capacities and delays, and direct-follow relationships mined from event logs with PM4Py, passed as markdown/JSON to the agents; plus a three-level adaptation complexity taxonomy [45]. AMBIGUITY: 'ontology' and 'knowledge-graph' would over-claim (no formal language, axioms or graph), and CPDs are company process requirements rather than published standards such as VDI or ISO, so 'standards-encoding' does not fit; coded 'other'. Contrast with the related work the authors cite, which does use knowledge graphs and the Asset Administration Shell [30,31].
column131: Executable simulation blueprint/template encoding production-system modelling semantics (machine, buffer, routing, schedule, failure and KPI logic) as a one-shot example, combined with structured critical process definitions (CPDs) as machine-checkable process constraints and process-mined direct-follow relationships as structured flow knowledge.
column134: An established simulation verification and validation framework is explicitly followed: 'we followed established verification and validation principles, including those recommended by Sargent [46]', with verification of model logic/flows/assumptions against the intended reference model, input-output validation via means and 95% confidence intervals over independent runs, predefined acceptable accuracy ranges for TH, SEC and WIP, identical input data across models, and an explicit two-part acceptance criterion - the reference value must fall inside the confidence interval or deviate by less than 10%, and no systematic bias may be present (Sections 4.4 and 5.6, pp. 648 and 655). This is complemented by author-defined output measures for the LLM component: per-stage code correctness, error typing (parametric/structural/scheduling/logic), and interpretation accuracy, tabulated per run and summarised in Fig. 18, plus token and cost accounting. AMBIGUITY: because the LLM-side measures are author-defined rather than standardised, R1 could instead code 'domain-specific-metric'; 'benchmark' does not fit (SWE-bench is cited only to select models, not to evaluate the artefact). Emerging LLM evaluation frameworks (Ragas [47], LLM-as-a-Judge [48]) are named only as future means of increasing testing capability (Section 6.1, p. 656) and were not applied.
column135: Sargent's simulation verification and validation framework [46] with predefined KPI accuracy thresholds (5-10%) and confidence-interval/no-systematic-bias acceptance criteria, combined with author-defined per-stage code-correctness and interpretation-accuracy tallies over repeated workflow executions.
column137: Score 3 - effectively replicable for Case B. Reported: the full four-stage workflow and agent roles (Figs. 1-4), the model-to-task assignment with selection rationale (Table 2), the explicit statement that default API parameters were used, two complete API calls with verbatim prompts (Listings 2-3), excerpts of the blueprint and of the generated models for both cases (Listings 1, 4, 5), the HITL checkpoints, machine parameter tables (Tables 4 and 6), event-log excerpt (Table 3), simulation horizons, warm-up and replication counts with their derivation, the validation protocol and thresholds, and per-run results with error typing (Tables 5 and 7). Decisively, 'the full implementation of the LLM-to-simulation pipeline, including blueprints, LLM calls, prompts, Python scripts, and input data for Case B is available at GitHub' (Section 4, p. 645). Residual gaps: Case A input data are not shared, Fig. 18 gives no numeric values, the criteria for judging an output 'correct' and who judged are not operationalised, and LLM non-determinism plus model deprecation limit exact reproduction - acknowledged by the authors themselves. Gaps concern verifiability of the evaluation rather than the method, hence 3 rather than 2; R1 could defend 2 on the unoperationalised correctness judgment.
column139: Score 3 - implemented system plus quantitative evaluation. The workflow was implemented and executed 21 times on two real production lines of a large Swedish automotive manufacturer, using real MES event logs for Case A, producing 4-5 executable simulation models per run; outcomes are quantified per workflow stage (code correctness, error type, adaptation and evaluation success; Tables 5, 7 and Fig. 18), the generated models are validated against manually built commercial-software reference models with reported relative deviations and predefined acceptance criteria (Tables 8, 9), and resource use is quantified (tokens, USD, runtime). Caveats that do not reduce the score below 3: author-performed outcome classification, a single case company, two comparatively simple lines, a mock-up event log for Case B, fictitious CPDs, no comparison against manual modelling effort or other ASMG methods, and no statistical testing of the KPI differences between adapted scenarios (the evaluator-agent itself recommends such testing).
column141: Score 3 - Q1 journal. Journal of Manufacturing Systems 85 (2026) 642-661, Elsevier for the Society of Manufacturing Engineers (ISSN 0278-6125). Scimago lists the journal as Q1 in Industrial and Manufacturing Engineering (best quartile Q1; SJR ~3.6, h-index 120), and it is indexed in WoS SCIE under Engineering Industrial, Engineering Manufacturing and Operations Research & Management Science.
